lessonRef.subject: mathematics
lessonRef.focus: everyday examples of conditional probability and independence
lessonRef.title: Skill consolidation: everyday examples of conditional probability and independence

sections.title: Independent practice
sections.directions: Work on your own. Show the steps that produced each answer.

items.prompt: Given P(A and B) = 4/20 and P(B) = 11/20, find P(A | B) as a fraction in lowest terms.
Given P(A) = 3/20, P(B) = 6/20, and P(A and B) = 2/20, find P(A or B) in lowest terms.
In a study, the probability of a delay is the same whether or not it is raining. What is the correct interpretation?
choices: The two conditional probabilities are equal, so the order of conditioning never matters.
The two events are mutually exclusive.
Delay and rain are independent, because conditioning on rain does not change the probability of a delay.
The relationship proves that one event causes the other.

items.prompt: A box holds 8 items, of which 6 are defective. Two are drawn without replacement. Find the probability that both are defective, in lowest terms.
Given P(A and B) = 49/100 and P(B) = 60/100, find P(A | B) as a fraction in lowest terms.
Given P(A) = 26/100, P(B) = 29/100, and P(A and B) = 7/100, find P(A or B) in lowest terms.
In a study, P(passes | attended the workshop) is higher than P(passes) overall. What is the correct interpretation?
choices: The two conditional probabilities are equal, so the order of conditioning never matters.
The two events are mutually exclusive.
Attendance and passing are associated, though this alone does not show that the workshop caused the improvement.
The relationship proves that one event causes the other.

items.prompt: A box holds 19 items, of which 17 are defective. Two are drawn without replacement. Find the probability that both are defective, in lowest terms.
Given P(A and B) = 1/100 and P(B) = 13/100, find P(A | B) as a fraction in lowest terms.

sections.title: Mastery check
sections.directions: Mastery check. Work without help, then stop and hand this section in.

items.prompt: Given P(A) = 6/20, P(B) = 9/20, and P(A and B) = 4/20, find P(A or B) in lowest terms.
In a study, P(has the condition | tested positive) is much smaller than P(tested positive | has the condition). What is the correct interpretation?
choices: The two conditional probabilities condition on different events, so they need not be close; a rare condition makes the first much smaller.
The two conditional probabilities are equal, so the order of conditioning never matters.
The two events are mutually exclusive.
The relationship proves that one event causes the other.
